[PAPER_0047, relevance_score=0.370] Our primary hypothesis (Hypothesis 1) tested the MMT, namely that changes in Decentering would predict changes in Reappraisal, resulting in changes in Well-being. We further hypothesized that, relative to an active control condition, well-being interventions with varied emphases on Decentering and Reappraisal including mindfulness training, reappraisal training, and a combined mindfulness and reappraisal training would promote Well-being via the MMT rather than acting upon Well-being directly.

[PAPER_0048, relevance_score=0.346] Changes From the Preregistration Plan

Several changes from the preregistration plan are noted. For the sake of parsimony, we moved several analyses (H2-H5) that were based on failed assumptions around intervention effects in H1 to the online supplemental materials . We review this decision and possible reasons for manipulation failures are in the discussion section. Additionally, four sets of post hoc, exploratory analyses were also performed. First, to directly test the mindful reappraisal hypothesis, we evaluated whether mindfulness training in the absence of positive reappraisal training increased Reappraisal.

[PAPER_0091, relevance_score=0.271] Preregistered Statistical Models

Model 1 evaluated the overall MMT model (Decentering → Reappraisal → Well-being) and the impact of intervention groups on Well-being at both the state and the trait level (i.e., intervention groups → Decentering → Reappraisal → Well-being). For the Group variable, all three active conditions (MC, SM, CC) were dummy coded against the AC condition.

[PAPER_0111, relevance_score=0.289] Changes From Preregistered Analyses

The SM condition only differed from the control (AC) condition at the level of within-session effects, but such reports did not generalize to the state or trait levels, suggesting no lasting impact of SM training on the MMT pathway. We therefore mad a post hoc decision to treat the SM condition as a second active control condition when exploring the effects of mindfulness training. We, therefore, refrain from detailing the remaining preregistered hypotheses comparing MC and SM, although these results are available in the online supplemental materials .

[PAPER_0121, relevance_score=0.228] We incorrectly predicted that Decentering's relationship with Well-being would be fully mediated by Reappraisal (the MMT pathway). Instead, only partial mediation was supported: in several mediation models, Decentering growth was directly linked to Well-being growth, with only 25%-40% of this effect mediated by Reappraisal.

items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0045, relevance_score=0.364] The Present Study

The primary aim of the study was to leverage existing online wellness interventions to evaluate the MMT pathway over a 3-week intervention period. To support causal inference, we focused on how randomization to interventions that targeted stages of the MMT predicted change in Decentering, Reappraisal, and Well-being. Theoretically consistent online interventions were designed: Decentering was targeted through mindfulness exercises, while Reappraisal was targeted through stress mindset exercises. The study was delivered entirely online through scheduled email links to maximize access and minimize intervention demands.

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.500] Participants

Participants were undergraduate students from the PSY100 Winter 2021 class at the University of Toronto Mississauga that were recruited via an online participant pool. As compensation, students were able to obtain up to 3% course credit toward their final grade in the course. The research protocol was approved by the University Research Ethics Board and is consistent with the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki. The average age of participants was 19.0 years, and 81.3% identified as female gender.

A priori power analysis was conducted before study enrollment to determine appropriate sample size.

[PAPER_0054, relevance_score=0.376] The simulation approach suggested that N = 171 was required.

Participant recruitment and flow through the study are summarized in a CONSORT diagram (Figure 2). Participants wishing to self-enroll were first screened via an online questionnaire using a web-based survey platform (Qualtrics, Provo, UT, United States).

[PAPER_0055, relevance_score=0.401] Participants were excluded for: (a) the presence of an ongoing cognitive or mood disorder, including substance use disorders, (b) previous diagnosis of such a disorder within the past year, (c) the absence of self-reported moderate to high levels of stress, and (d) inability to commit to participating in the required study sessions. Based on these criteria, 24 students were excluded from the study before entering the informed consent process. The remaining sample (n = 155) completed baseline questionnaires and informed consent. Missing data were represented by the symbol NA (not available) and not manipulated.

[PAPER_0063, relevance_score=0.319] MC Condition

The mindfulness with choice (MC) condition involved similar training materials from our previous study (Wang & Farb, 2023; more information is available in the online supplemental materials ), which introduced participants to mindfulness meditation, featuring exercises to focus attention on the internal sensation of the body or the breath with a nonjudgmental, curious attitude. Training videos, which were based on mindfulness-based interventions (e.g., body scan, mindful breathing), were recorded and uploaded onto Qualtrics for online asynchronous learning by the current researchers.

[PAPER_0096, relevance_score=0.330] Baseline Moderators and Well-being

The impact of baseline measure scores on changes in daily (state) Well-being was evaluated using Day × Baseline Moderator multilevel models.

Further methodological details are available in the online supplemental materials .

items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0068, relevance_score=0.439] Trait Measures: Across the Study Period

Trait measures were assessed via self-report questionnaires administered at two-time points: baseline and postintervention. We preregistered three planned composite outcome variables: Well-being, Coping, and Symptom Burden. Composite scores were created via the factor analysis function (fa) in R, which gives standardized scores and is mean-centered. As Coping and Symptom Burden were not the primary target outcome variables, they are discussed in the online supplemental materials .

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.361] Four measures were each operationalized using a single validated questionnaire: Stress Mindset, Mindfulness, Decentering, and Reappraisal.

[PAPER_0074, relevance_score=0.320] Mindfulness

Mindfulness was assessed using the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire-15 (FFMQ-15; Baer et al., 2008), which is a short form of the 39-item FFMQ measuring five facets: Observing, Describing, Acting with Awareness, Nonjudging, and Nonreactivity. Higher scores indicated better mindfulness skills. Participants rated each item from 1 (never or rarely true) to 5 (often or always true), with good internal consistency (α = 0.81).

[PAPER_0075, relevance_score=0.301] Decentering

Decentering was measured using the Metacognitive Processes of Decentering-Trait (MPoD-t; Hanley et al., 2020), which captures meta-awareness, (dis)identification with internal experience, and (non)reactivity to internal experience. Participants rated items from 1 (never or very rarely) to 5 (very often or always). Higher scores indicated better decentering skills. Internal consistency was good (α = 0.88).

[PAPER_0082, relevance_score=0.312] Decentering

The measure consisted of two questions (from the MPoD-t) "I can watch my thoughts and emotions come and go like clouds" and "I am more than my thoughts and feelings." Respondents rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Internal consistency was good (α = 0.84).

[PAPER_0091, relevance_score=0.443] Preregistered Statistical Models

Model 1 evaluated the overall MMT model (Decentering → Reappraisal → Well-being) and the impact of intervention groups on Well-being at both the state and the trait level (i.e., intervention groups → Decentering → Reappraisal → Well-being). For the Group variable, all three active conditions (MC, SM, CC) were dummy coded against the AC condition.

[PAPER_0092, relevance_score=0.374] Exploratory Models of Intervention Effects

Effect of Mindfulness and Reappraisal Training

Before proceeding to evaluate the planned MMT SEM models, we assessed Group × Time interactions on each of the main MMT variables (Decentering, Reappraisal, and Well-being) at the session, state, and trait levels.

[PAPER_0094, relevance_score=0.372] Specifically, we modeled autocorrelation and cross-correlation between Decentering and Reappraisal with each variable's next timepoint (∼3 or 4 days between training sessions), nesting data within participants to also model participant-specific random effects (the complete model specification is available in the online supplemental materials ). This model allowed a simultaneous test of whether Decentering predicted subsequent Reappraisal, and whether Reappraisal predicted subsequent Decentering, while controlling for autoregression (each variable subsequently predicting itself) and participant-specific random effects.

[PAPER_0099, relevance_score=0.337] The MMT Pathway

Hypothesis 1 tested the MMT pathway, linking change in Decentering to Reappraisal to Well-being (Figure 3). Decentering was positively associated with Reappraisal and Reappraisal with Well-being at all three levels of analysis. Model fit was satisfactory by CFI, indicating a good fit relative to a null model. However, the fit was poor according to the RMSEA. Subsequent model exploration suggested that a just-identified model was superior, which included a direct path from Decentering to Well-being.

[PAPER_0067, relevance_score=0.333] Measures

Many of the explanatory and outcome variables in the study were operationalized as preregistered composite measures, which were constructed using factor analysis via the "psych" package (Revelle, 2017). For each composite variable, the adequacy of a single factor to summarize the questionnaires used was confirmed using Horn's Test of Principal Components and applied to questionnaire scores using the "paran" package (Dinno, 2012) in R.

[PAPER_0068, relevance_score=0.310] Trait Measures: Across the Study Period

Trait measures were assessed via self-report questionnaires administered at two-time points: baseline and postintervention. We preregistered three planned composite outcome variables: Well-being, Coping, and Symptom Burden. Composite scores were created via the factor analysis function (fa) in R, which gives standardized scores and is mean-centered. As Coping and Symptom Burden were not the primary target outcome variables, they are discussed in the online supplemental materials .

[PAPER_0086, relevance_score=0.342] To simplify model fitting, we modeled change scores for all variables prior to entry into SEM analysis to test a series of preregistered models (Wang, Garland, & Farb, 2023; https://osf.io/c2xzd). While ideally modeling the relationship between such changes would occur in a single modeling step, power simulations for latent change score models suggest they may several times the sample size needed to detect individual growth curves (Zhang & Liu, 2018), far exceeding the present sample size.

[PAPER_0087, relevance_score=0.356] Trait (baseline and postintervention) and session (pre- and postsession) change scores were modeled as simple difference scores. State-level change scores were modeled as participant-specific random effects (slopes) of time in a multilevel model using the package "lme4" (Bates et al., 2015) in the R statistical programming environment (R Core Team, 2013).

To conduct the SEM analyses, we used the "lavaan" package in R (Rosseel, 2012).

[PAPER_0093, relevance_score=0.321] Lagged Regression of Decentering and Reappraisal

Given that prior tests of the MMT pathway employed primarily cross-sectional correlational methods, it was important to leverage the many time points within the current study to explore whether there was evidence for Decentering leading to Reappraisal. We, therefore, conducted a multivariate multilevel model to explore the within-participant coupling of the two constructs. We followed recommendations for intensive longitudinal modeling (Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013) as implemented in R (Ram, n.d.).
